balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Molina Healthcare, Inc.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Molina Healthcare, Inc.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Molina Healthcare, Inc.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Molina Healthcare, Inc.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Molina Healthcare, Inc.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

mcr.title: Medical Care Ratio
mcr.content:
The Medical Care Ratio (MCR) is medical costs paid out divided by premium revenue -- the health-insurer equivalent of a combined ratio. Lower is more profitable, but a government-contract insurer can be penalized or forced to issue rebates if it runs too low.

For Molina Healthcare, Inc.: Molina's margin comes almost entirely from the spread between capitated Medicaid/Medicare rates and actual medical cost trend; MCR is the single number that tells you whether rate increases from state and CMS contracts are keeping pace with utilization and acuity.

What to watch:

  • MCR drifting up through the year as acuity or utilization trend runs hot (common after Medicaid redetermination unwinds a healthier risk pool)
  • Minimum MCR / medical-loss-ratio rebate thresholds in state contracts
  • Divergence from peers' reported MCR in the same state book

membership.title: Membership by program
membership.content:
Membership is the number of enrolled lives Molina administers, split by government program.

For Molina Healthcare, Inc.: Medicaid membership moves with state redetermination cycles (eligibility re-checks that can shed members quickly) and new state contract wins/losses; Medicare membership is smaller but higher-margin per member and grows mostly through M&A and AEP enrollment. A membership drop with flat or rising premium revenue usually means rate increases, not volume, are driving growth.

What to watch:

  • Medicaid redetermination-driven attrition versus new contract starts
  • Medicare membership growth rate relative to the Medicaid base
  • Member mix shifting toward the higher-acuity, higher-MCR cohort

segmentRevenue.title: Premium revenue by segment
segmentRevenue.content:
Premium revenue by segment shows how much of Molina's top line comes from each government program.

For Molina Healthcare, Inc.: Medicaid is the core, state-contract-driven book; Medicare and Marketplace/other are the smaller but faster-growing lines management points to for diversification. Watch this alongside the membership chart -- revenue growing faster than membership in a segment means rate, not volume, is doing the work.

What to watch:

  • Concentration in Medicaid and exposure to state contract re-procurements
  • Medicare/Marketplace share of the mix trending up as a diversification signal
  • Segment revenue growth versus segment MCR (growth funded by underpricing is not real growth)

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Molina Healthcare, Inc.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Molina Healthcare, Inc.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Molina Healthcare, Inc.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Molina Healthcare, Inc.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Molina Healthcare, Inc.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
